name: Concealer (for men)

lead: Concealer is a thick, highly pigmented makeup used on small areas, most often to mask under-eye dark circles, spots, redness and scars. The evened-out tone shows immediately, and men use it as a quick, low-cost way to look fresher and reduce the look of eye bags.

Its pigment sits on top of the skin and blocks or neutralises the darker or redder tone beneath. Makeup guides describe yellow or peach tones for dark circles, green for redness such as pimples or rosacea, and a shade one or two steps lighter than the skin for brightening. Research on concealer itself is sparse and mostly not specific to men.

paras: It comes as liquid, cream, stick, pencil and cream-to-powder, and is blended in with fingers, a brush or a sponge, on its own or over or under foundation. Men discuss using small amounts to keep it discreet.

Concealer is a cosmetic generally sold without prescription. Some products contain ingredients such as fragrance, mineral oil, dimethicone or talc, which can bother sensitive skin. A 2021 questionnaire study of 539 Korean adults examined links between cosmetic use and acne. It covers the look of dark circles and blemishes while worn and does not change their cause.

chain: Dark circles and blemishes blend away
angle.text: Men use concealer to cover under-eye circles, blemishes and redness, and the evened-out tone is visible straight away. Pigment on the skin blocks the darker or redder colour underneath; male-specific research is limited.

lead: Concealer is a cosmetic used to mask skin imperfections such as dark under-eye circles, blemishes, redness and hyperpigmentation. It is similar to foundation but more heavily pigmented, applied in small amounts to the specific area and blended with a brush, sponge or fingertips [1]. For men, it is the product most often described as an entry point into makeup: a small tube of skin-toned or colour-corrected pigment that can make a face look more rested and even without changing how the rest of it looks.

Products come in liquid, stick, cream, pencil and cream-to-powder forms, and colour theory is part of their use: yellow and peach tones are used over dark circles, green over redness, and a shade a step or two lighter than the skin is commonly chosen for brightening [1]. In looksmaxxing forums concealer is discussed mostly as an inexpensive, immediate way to reduce the look of eye bags and uneven skin, alongside threads about doing it discreetly [2][3][4].

Concealer has a documented lineage in film makeup and in medical camouflage cosmetics, and survey research since 2019 reports that concealer is among the products men are most willing to try [5][6]. Published clinical research on concealer itself is small and mostly involves women or mixed patient groups; no study tests it in men specifically [7][8].

paras: A concealer is formulated with more pigment than a foundation, so a small amount covers a small area. Wikipedia lists common ingredients including castor seed oil, dimethicone, glycerin, talc, kaolin, mineral oil, fragrance and colour additives [1]. It can be applied before foundation to build an even base, after foundation to touch up spots that need more coverage, or on its own [1].
Camouflage makeup, used for birthmarks, scars and vitiligo, is described as a much heavier-pigmented relative of everyday concealer [1].

Wikipedia describes liquid concealer, sold in tubes or vials with satin, radiant or matte finishes, as the most popular form and suited to most skin types, with powder commonly used to set it. Stick concealer is thicker and gives high coverage for small areas and touch-ups. Cream concealer comes in a pot or palette with opaque coverage and is often applied with a brush; pencil concealer is creamy or wax-based for small spots and can also define brows; cream-to-powder compacts give a matte finish and are applied with a sponge [1].

An AI-generated encyclopedia entry adds that liquid concealers tend to be lightweight and buildable, creams more emollient and suited to dry skin, and sticks portable but prone to sliding on oily skin without powder; this entry is machine-written and should be read with caution [9].

People often choose a shade one or two steps lighter than their skin, according to Wikipedia. Yellow-toned concealers are used for dark circles, green and blue tones counteract redness from pimples, broken veins or rosacea, and purple tints are said to brighten sallow complexions [1]. The same complementary-colour principle underlies the 'colour corrector' products sold in green and peach tones [9].
Forum users stress shade match: one commenter on a looksmax.org concealer thread wrote that the wrong colour can look obvious and uncanny [2].

Wikipedia's article on periorbital dark circles lists a range of contributors: bony structure and thin lower-eyelid skin, allergies and rubbing, medications that dilate vessels, iron or vitamin deficiency, fatigue, ageing, sun exposure, heredity and bruising [10]. A 2021 clinic study of 100 patients classified dark circles as constitutional, post-inflammatory, vascular, shadow effects or others, and found that patient dissatisfaction rose with clinical severity, with higher Fitzpatrick skin type, and with fewer hours of sleep [8].
Because the causes differ, medical sources describe separate treatments such as topical ingredients, lasers or fillers, whereas concealer addresses only the appearance [10].

Wikipedia dates the first commercially available concealer to Max Factor's Erace, launched in 1954 [1]. Max Factor's own article places the company's origins in theatrical and film makeup: Max Factor Sr. moved to Los Angeles in 1904, was developing flexible greasepaint by 1914, and built a business supplying Hollywood; Pan-Cake foundation, created for Technicolor, followed later [11].

A parallel strand is corrective cosmetics for visible skin differences. Lydia O'Leary (1900-1982), born with a large port-wine stain on her face, patented a foundation for covering birthmarks and discolourations in 1932 and founded Covermark; her company later worked with plastic surgeons and dermatologists on camouflage for war wounds and, in the 1980s, marketed to men and children as well as women [12]. A 1988 article in the dermatology journal Cutis discussed the need for, evaluation of and use of corrective cosmetics [13].

Men's makeup more broadly has a long history: Wikipedia traces male eye paint to ancient Egypt and powdered faces to Elizabethan England, notes its reappearance in 1930s American film, and says men's beauty products were largely absent from mainstream retail until the late 1990s [14].

A Morning Consult survey of 2,142 US men fielded in September 2019 found that 33% of men aged 18-29 and 23% of all men would consider wearing makeup; cover-up, concealer and tinted moisturiser ranked highest among products men would try, ahead of blush and mascara [5]. Founders quoted in the same report named easing stigma, social-media pressure to look polished and the privacy of online shopping as drivers [5].

An Ipsos survey of US heterosexual men published in 2022 found 15% of men aged 18-65 used male cosmetics and a further 17% would consider it. Men aged 18-34 were more open to BB/CC creams, mascara, foundation, bronzer and concealer than older men, and said they wanted to attract partners and cover blemishes; men over 50 more often cited looking younger or more professional and wanted discreet ways to buy [6].

CNBC coverage republished by The Nightly describes concealer as the usual first purchase, often followed by primer, setting powder and tinted SPF, and names men-focused brands such as War Paint, Stryx, TONE and Papatui. It cites Statista data that the share of US men who never wear makeup fell from over 90% in 2019 to about 75% in 2024, and quotes a Sukoshi executive saying the biggest barrier is uncertainty rather than price [15]. Wikipedia's article on male cosmetics notes that influencers such as Patrick Starr and James Charles are prominent, and that cosmetics remain less accepted for men than for women [14].

On looksmax.org, one poster describes concealer as probably the best 'looksmax' for people with naturally persistent under-eye darkness and posts before-and-after photos, saying the difference is more noticeable in person; replies include that it can also cover squint wrinkles, that the colour must match, and a view that concealer is where the line should be drawn before other makeup [2].

Other threads concern social aspects: members ask how to buy and keep concealer without family noticing [3], whether wearing it carries stigma [16], and one member recounts a parent noticing product on his chin hair after he slept with it on [17]. A thread titled as a makeup guide for men collects further tips [4].

Concealer is sold as an over-the-counter cosmetic. A 2021 questionnaire study of 539 patients with acne at three Korean clinics found that 38.1% of those whose acne treatment had failed said continued cosmetic use worsened their acne, versus 26.3% of treatment-naive patients; liquid foundation and concealer were frequently used in the treatment-failure group, and the authors suggested dermatologists advise acne patients about cosmetic use [18].
A 2020 laboratory study formulated an anti-acne concealer containing cinnamon oil and tested its activity against acne-associated bacteria in vitro [19].

No studies found that test concealer in men specifically. Related published work includes a 2021 programme in 30 women (mean age 42) using a full-coverage concealer on bruising after injectables or threads, in which clinicians rated 78.18% of users as having clear skin with no erythema after application, no product-related adverse events were reported over about two weeks, and 98.81% of subjects were at least slightly satisfied [7].

The 2021 dark-circle study of 100 patients (Johns Hopkins and Seattle) found that use of concealer was among the factors correlated with subjective dissatisfaction (r=0.35), alongside female sex, higher Fitzpatrick type and fewer sleep hours; correlation does not show which came first [8]. The 2021 Korean acne questionnaire and a 1988 article on corrective cosmetics complete the published record around concealer use [18][13].
